title: OLTP vs OLAP and Columnar Storage
lesson:
Databases serve two very different workloads. OLTP (online transaction processing) handles many small, latency-sensitive operations that touch a few rows at a time: place an order, update a profile, look up an account. OLAP (online analytical processing) runs fewer but much heavier queries that scan large portions of a table and aggregate a handful of columns: total revenue by region over the last year. Their access patterns pull storage design in opposite directions.

Row-oriented storage keeps all columns of a row together on disk. That layout is ideal for OLTP, because reading or writing one whole record is a single contiguous access, and inserts are cheap. Column-oriented storage keeps each column's values together instead. An analytical query that needs only 3 of 100 columns reads just those 3 columns' data rather than every full row, cutting I/O dramatically.

Columnar layout has a second advantage: values within a column are the same type and often similar, so they compress very well using techniques like run-length encoding, dictionary encoding, and delta encoding. Compressed columns also let engines process data in batches (vectorized execution) and skip blocks using per-block min/max statistics. The cost is that writing or fetching a single full row means touching many separate column files, so point updates and single-row inserts are comparatively expensive.

Because of this tradeoff, production systems commonly keep the two separate: an OLTP database serves the application, and data is copied into a columnar warehouse (via batch ETL or change data capture) for analytics. This also keeps heavy scans from competing with user-facing transactions for the same resources.

questions.prompt: Why does columnar storage speed up analytical queries like 'sum of revenue by region'?
options: It stores data in memory only
The query reads only the needed columns instead of every full row
questions.explanation: Analytical queries touch few columns across many rows, and columnar layout lets the engine read just those columns, reducing I/O.

questions.prompt: Row-oriented storage is generally a better fit for OLTP workloads that read or write whole records.
questions.explanation: Keeping a row's columns contiguous makes fetching or writing one full record a single access, which suits OLTP.

questions.prompt: Storing each column's values together compresses well because values in a column share the same ____.
questions.explanation: Same-typed, often similar values in a column enable encodings like run-length and dictionary encoding that compress effectively.

questions.prompt: Order the typical flow that feeds an analytics warehouse, earliest first.
items: Analysts run large aggregate queries on columnar storage
Changes are extracted via ETL or change data capture
The application writes transactions to the OLTP database
Data is loaded into the columnar warehouse
questions.explanation: Transactions land in the OLTP store, changes are extracted, loaded into the warehouse, and only then queried analytically.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of columnar storage?
options: Expensive single-row inserts and updates, since a row spans many column files
questions.explanation: A full row is split across per-column storage, so point writes and whole-row reads touch many locations.
